Catching Stolen Cars with Math

How Statistics Helps Police Find Stolen Vehicles — and Leave Innocent Drivers Alone

Jessica Minnier, OHSU Knight Cancer Institute

2026-05-14

Today’s Question

How can math help police catch more stolen cars

while pulling over fewer innocent drivers?

Welcome! Today we’ll walk through a real data science project. You’ll see ideas from AP Stats (proportions, odds, models) but I’ll define everything as we go. ~15 min plus discussion.

Who Am I?

  • Jessica Minnier, biostatistician at OHSU (Oregon Health & Science University)
  • I mostly study cancer data 🧬
  • But the same statistical tools work for almost any “predict an outcome from clues” problem
  • Today’s project: data from Portland Police Bureau Stolen Vehicle Operations (SVO)

Statistics is a transferable superpower. 🦸

The Problem

Cars get stolen. A lot.

  • Police want to recover them
  • They can’t pull over every car
  • Pulling over innocent drivers is bad: wastes time, scares people, damages trust

Goal:

Pull over the cars most likely to be stolen.

Leave the rest alone.

How? With DATA.

What Officers Record on Each Stop

When police make a stop during a stolen vehicle operation (SVO), they record:

  • Outcomes: Was the car stolen? Were there warrants? Was a gun recovered?
  • “Enrichment factors”: observable clues before the stop
  • Vehicle info: make, model, year, color

Each row of the dataset = one stop. As of November 2025, we have 1,930 stops across 5 agencies.

“Enrichment factors” is the police term for “observable warning signs this car might be stolen” — things you can see from outside the car.

What’s an “Enrichment Factor”?

A clue police can spot from outside the car. There are 39 of them. Examples:

License plates:

  • Missing front plate
  • Missing back plate
  • Plate doesn’t match the car
  • Plate reported stolen

Vehicle behavior / appearance:

  • Eluding police (running)
  • Broken windows
  • Tinted windows
  • Driver hiding their face

The big question: do these clues actually predict stolen?

Picture the Data Structure

1 row = 1 stop. Columns = clues + outcome.
Stop Elude Broken windows Stolen plate More clues Stolen?
#1 Yes No No … YES
#2 No No No … NO
#3 Yes Yes Yes … YES
#4 Yes No No … NO
… … … … … …

This shape — rows = observations, columns = variables — is what all of statistics works with.

The Sample Grew Over Time

Sample size growing over time
Period Stops Agencies Cumulative
Mar 2022 – Oct 2022 561 PPB only 561
Oct 2022 – Apr 2023 255 PPB only 816
Apr 2023 – Dec 2023 428 PPB only 1244
Jan 2024 – Aug 2024 334 PPB only 1578
Sept 2024 – Nov 2025 352 PPB + 4 more agencies 1930

More data → more reliable estimates. Adding other agencies (Gresham, Multnomah County, etc.) lets us check whether patterns hold beyond just Portland.

⚠️ But this is not a random sample of all cars on the road — these cars were already flagged as suspicious. A key idea in AP Stats: sampling bias affects what we can conclude.

A Proportion Is Just a Fraction

\[ \text{proportion} = \frac{\text{count of "yes"}}{\text{total count}} \]

In our data of 1,930 stops:

  • ~28% of stopped vehicles were stolen
  • ~21% had outstanding warrants
  • ~5% had a gun recovered

So among SVO stops, roughly 1 in 4 ends up being a stolen car. Can we do better?

Comparing Proportions: Does a Clue Help?

Among cars where the driver eluded police:

  • ~55% turned out to be stolen

Among cars that did NOT elude:

  • ~21% turned out to be stolen

Eluding police more than doubles the proportion stolen. That’s a strong signal!

From Proportions to Odds

Tip

  • Proportion (or probability): out of everyone, how many “yes”?
    • \(P = \dfrac{\text{stolen}}{\text{stolen} + \text{not stolen}}\)
  • Odds: ratio of “yes” to “no”
    • \(\text{odds} = \dfrac{\text{stolen}}{\text{not stolen}} = \dfrac{P}{1-P}\)

If 55% are stolen: odds = \(\frac{0.55}{0.45} \approx 1.22\) (a bit more than 1-to-1)

If 21% are stolen: odds = \(\frac{0.21}{0.79} \approx 0.27\) (about 1-to-4)

Why Odds? Because of Odds Ratios (OR)

\[ \text{Odds Ratio} = \frac{\text{odds of stolen WITH the clue}}{\text{odds of stolen WITHOUT the clue}} \]

For “elude”: \(\text{OR} = \dfrac{1.22}{0.27} \approx 4.5\)

Interpretation: A car that eludes police has about 4.5× higher odds of being stolen than one that doesn’t.

  • OR = 1 → the clue doesn’t matter
  • OR > 1 → the clue raises odds of stolen
  • OR < 1 → the clue lowers odds of stolen

Reading an Odds Ratio Plot

The horizontal line is a confidence interval — the range of plausible values. If it crosses 1, the clue may not really matter.

What If a Car Has Several Clues?

A real car might be eluding police AND have a broken window AND missing plates.

Do all three clues each add information? Or do they overlap?

We need a model that uses all the clues together.

What’s a “Model” with Predictors and an Outcome?

A statistical model is a rule that takes in predictors (inputs / clues) and estimates the chance of an outcome.

\[ \color{#c0392b}{P(\text{Stolen})} = f(\color{#0E4D92}{\text{plates, windows, elude, } \ldots}) \]

red = outcome  ·  blue = predictors

Think of it like a recipe:

  • Ingredients → predictors (the clues)
  • Recipe → the model (the math)
  • Dish → the predicted probability of being stolen

Logistic Regression: The Engine

For yes/no outcomes (stolen / not stolen), the workhorse model is logistic regression.

The model assigns each clue a weight:

\[ \log(\text{odds of stolen}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{clue}_1 + \beta_2 \cdot \text{clue}_2 + \dots \]

  • \(\beta > 0\): clue raises stolen odds
  • \(\beta < 0\): clue lowers stolen odds
  • \(e^{\beta}\) = the odds ratio (the thing we just learned!)

Don’t worry about the algebra — the idea is what matters: each clue gets a weight.

With 39 Clues, We Have a Problem 😬

  • We have 39 enrichment factors
  • Some are redundant (e.g., “elude high-speed” and “elude into blocks” usually go together)
  • Including all 39 can make the model overfit — it memorizes our specific data and fails on new cars
  • We need a way to keep only the most useful clues

Enter the LASSO 🤠

Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator

A clever twist on logistic regression that:

  1. Tries to fit the data well (like regular regression), AND
  2. Penalizes the model for having too many predictors

Less-useful clues get their weight squeezed all the way to zero — the LASSO drops them automatically.

Result: Out of 39 factors, 24 were kept. The other 15 didn’t add much once the strong clues were in.

What the LASSO Picked

Surprises in the Data

  • Tinted windows lowered the odds — many factory tints aren’t a real signal
  • Expired plates strongly lowered odds — that’s people who forgot to renew, not car thieves
  • Plate already flagged stolen raises odds by ~35× — the clearest possible clue

Statistics helps us separate real signals from false ones — including some that people might have assumed mattered but actually don’t.

Is the Model Any Good?

The model gives every car a predicted probability of being stolen, from 0% to 100%.

We measure overall accuracy with one number, called AUC — short for “area under the curve.”

AUC value Quality
0.5 Coin flip — useless
0.7 Okay
0.88 Our stolen-vehicle model ✅
1.0 Perfect (and unrealistic)

What Could This Mean in Practice?

  • Without the model, only ~28% of stops were stolen cars
  • With the model guiding decisions, that hit rate could rise to ~65%
  • Fewer innocent drivers pulled over
  • More stolen cars taken off the road

A small statistical idea → a real-world impact.

Fairness Matters Too ⚖️

Important

A model that’s “accurate” overall can still be unfair to certain groups.

  • We checked whether predicted probabilities behave similarly across groups of drivers
  • Enrichment factors are about the vehicle, not the driver — that helps
  • This is ongoing work

Statistics doesn’t just answer “does it work?” — it also asks “does it work fairly?”

What We Did Today

  1. Saw real data structure — rows of stops, columns of clues and outcomes
  2. Compared proportions to see which clues raise the chance of stolen
  3. Turned proportions into odds and odds ratios
  4. Built a logistic regression model with multiple predictors
  5. Used LASSO to automatically pick the most useful clues
  6. Checked accuracy with AUC

The Big Idea

Statistics turns clues + outcomes into better decisions.

The same recipe works for:

  • 🧬 Predicting which patients respond to a cancer drug
  • 🎬 Recommending movies you might like
  • 🌧️ Forecasting whether it’ll rain tomorrow
  • 🤖 Pretty much any “predict from features” problem in machine learning

If you took AP Stats — this is what the rest of the iceberg looks like. 🧊

Questions to Think About 🤔

  • What would happen if our data only came from one type of neighborhood?
  • Could a model be technically accurate but still cause harm?
  • Who should decide when to use the model? Police? Community? Data scientists?
  • What clues aren’t in the data that might matter?
